sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Use GitLab CI/CD variables safely: predefined and custom variables, masked and protected values, group-level and scoped variables, and precedence rules.

As soon as a pipeline becomes useful, it needs data. A build may need the current branch name. A deploy job may need a cloud token. A Docker publish step may need a registry URL. A staging deployment may need one database connection string, while production needs another. This is where GitLab CI/CD variables become essential.

This tutorial explains GitLab CI variables, secrets, and environments in depth. You will learn what variables are, why they matter, which predefined variables are most useful, how to define custom variables in different places, how precedence works when values collide, how masked and protected variables improve security, how environment-scoped variables solve staging-versus-production differences, how group-level variables help teams reuse configuration across projects, how to reference variables in Linux and Windows scripts, how to pass values between jobs with a dotenv artifact, and how to handle multi-line credentials with file-type variables.

sections.title: What Are CI/CD Variables and Why Do They Matter?
paragraphs: A CI/CD variable is a named value available to pipeline jobs at runtime.
Instead of hard-coding values into your repository, you inject them when the pipeline runs. That makes pipelines safer, more flexible, and easier to reuse.
Variables can represent:
If you place secrets directly in .gitlab-ci.yml or source code, you create obvious risks:
Variables let you keep sensitive or changing values outside the committed application logic.

sections.title: Predefined Variables in GitLab CI
paragraphs: GitLab automatically provides many predefined variables during pipeline execution. These variables describe the project, commit, branch, pipeline, environment, and registry context.
You do not define them yourself. GitLab injects them when jobs run.
Here are some of the most useful predefined variables for beginners.
CI_COMMIT_BRANCH contains the branch name that triggered the pipeline.
Use it when you want branch-aware behavior, such as:
CI_COMMIT_SHA contains the full commit SHA for the pipeline's revision.
This is incredibly useful for:
CI_PROJECT_NAME gives you the project name. It is helpful for logs, dynamic file names, or reusable scripts that behave differently depending on the project context.
CI_PIPELINE_ID is a unique numeric identifier for the pipeline.
This is useful when you want:
CI_REGISTRY points to the container registry associated with GitLab.
If you are building and pushing container images, this variable helps avoid hard-coding registry locations.
CI_ENVIRONMENT_NAME becomes especially useful in deployment jobs that define an environment such as staging or production.
It lets scripts know which environment they are targeting.
These built-in values make pipelines context-aware without requiring manual configuration for every run. They are the foundation for reusable automation.

codeBlock.code:
script:
  - echo "Running on branch $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH"

sections.title: Defining Custom Variables in .gitlab-ci.yml
paragraphs: Not every value comes from GitLab automatically. You will often define your own custom variables.
One place to do this is directly in .gitlab-ci.yml.
You can define variables at the top level so many jobs can reuse them:
These values are easy to use across jobs.
You can also define variables only for a specific job:
This keeps configuration close to the job that needs it.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Where should I store secrets in GitLab CI?

In project, group or instance CI/CD variables, marked both masked and protected, never in .gitlab-ci.yml, which is committed to the repository and visible to anyone with read access. Masking keeps the value out of job logs and protection restricts it to protected branches and tags, so a merge request from a fork cannot read your production credentials. For higher-value secrets, GitLab integrates with external managers such as HashiCorp Vault so the pipeline fetches a short-lived credential at run time rather than holding a long-lived one.
What is the difference between masked and protected variables?

Masking replaces the value with [MASKED] wherever it would appear in a job log, which prevents accidental disclosure through debug output. Protection restricts the variable to jobs running on protected branches and protected tags, so ordinary feature branches and merge requests never receive it. They solve different problems and production secrets should have both: masking alone still exposes the value to any branch, and protection alone still risks printing it into a log.
Why is my masked variable not being masked?

GitLab can only mask values that meet its requirements: a minimum length, a single line, and no characters outside the supported set. A value with spaces, newlines or unusual punctuation is rejected for masking, and GitLab tells you so when you save it rather than silently failing. Base64-encoding an awkward value is the usual workaround. Note that masking only covers exact matches: if a script transforms the secret before printing it, the transformed form appears in the log unmasked.
Which variable wins when the same name is defined in several places?

The most specific definition wins. Roughly, from lowest to highest precedence: instance variables, then group, then project, then variables defined in .gitlab-ci.yml at the top level, then job-level variables, and finally values passed when manually triggering a pipeline or by a trigger token. Predefined variables that GitLab supplies cannot be overridden. When a value is not what you expect, printing it in a throwaway job is the quickest way to confirm which layer supplied it.
How do I pass a variable from one job to another?

Write it to a dotenv file and expose that file as a dotenv report artifact. Variables in it are then automatically available as environment variables in subsequent jobs, which is the supported way to hand a computed value, a generated image tag, a deployment URL, a version number, down the pipeline. Plain export does not work, because each job runs in its own container and shell with no shared state.
Can merge requests from forks access my secrets?

Not if the variables are marked protected, which is exactly what protection is for. An unprotected variable is available to any pipeline including those from forked repositories, which means an untrusted contributor could add a job that prints it. This is the single most important reason to mark production credentials protected as well as masked, and to review changes to .gitlab-ci.yml in merge requests from outside your organisation with particular care.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn what a GitLab Runner is and how it runs jobs: shared versus specific runners, executors, installing and registering on Ubuntu, and a Docker executor.

A GitLab Runner is the worker process that actually executes the jobs you define in .gitlab-ci.yml. GitLab itself stores your repository, reads your pipeline definition, calculates which jobs should run, and shows the results in the UI. The runner is the agent that picks up one of those jobs, prepares an execution environment, runs the commands, collects logs, uploads artifacts, and reports the status back to GitLab. If GitLab CI/CD is the brain of your automation system, the runner is the pair of hands doing the work.

This distinction matters because many GitLab beginners assume that adding a job to .gitlab-ci.yml is enough by itself. In reality, GitLab needs available runners. Without a runner, jobs remain stuck in a pending state. That is why understanding GitLab CI runner architecture, GitLab runner types, and GitLab runner registration is essential for building reliable pipelines.

sections.title: What Is a GitLab Runner and Why It Exists
paragraphs: GitLab pipelines are declarative. You describe stages, jobs, rules, images, artifacts, environments, and deployment behavior in YAML. But YAML does not execute itself. GitLab therefore relies on the GitLab Runner application, which can be installed on Linux, Windows, macOS, virtual machines, cloud hosts, or Kubernetes nodes.
A runner exists for a few practical reasons:

When a pipeline starts, GitLab places jobs into a queue. Runners poll GitLab for matching jobs. A runner only picks up a job if the job matches its scope and tags, and if the runner is allowed to execute it. Once assigned, the runner prepares the job environment, checks out the repository, restores cache if configured, runs the job script, uploads artifacts, and returns either success or failure.

sections.title: Types of GitLab Runners
paragraphs: When people search for shared runner GitLab, group runner, or specific runner GitLab, they are really asking who a runner belongs to and which projects may use it.

Shared runners are available to many projects. On GitLab.com, shared runners are the easiest way to get started because GitLab hosts and manages them for you. You do not need to install anything. If your project is allowed to use shared runners, your jobs can start immediately.
Shared runners are convenient for:
However, shared runners also come with tradeoffs:
That is why many companies start with shared runners for development workloads and move critical deployment jobs to self-hosted runners.
Group runners are attached at the GitLab group level and can be used by projects within that group. This is a good middle ground between convenience and control.
Use group runners when:
Group runners are especially helpful in monorepos or in organizations with many microservices using the same language stack.
A project-specific runner is registered for one project only. This is often the safest and most controlled option.
Use project runners when:
If your project deploys to production or touches highly sensitive infrastructure, a project-specific runner is often a better design than relying on shared runners.

sections.title: GitLab Runner Executor Types
paragraphs: The next major concept is the GitLab runner executor. The executor determines how the job runs.
The shell executor runs job commands directly on the host machine using Bash, PowerShell, or another supported shell.
The shell executor is fine for trusted internal jobs, but it is usually not the best default for multi-tenant CI.

The Docker executor is the most popular option. Each job runs inside a container created from the configured image. That gives you clean, repeatable environments and makes language-specific builds straightforward.

The docker+machine executor creates temporary Docker hosts on demand, traditionally using Docker Machine. Conceptually, this gives you elastic runners that spin up new machines for jobs and tear them down later.
In modern GitLab environments, many teams now prefer Kubernetes-based autoscaling rather than older Docker Machine workflows, but the concept is still worth knowing.
The Kubernetes executor launches each CI job as a pod in a Kubernetes cluster.
The SSH executor connects to an external machine over SSH and runs commands there.

This clean-slate behavior reduces the “works on one runner, fails on another” problem.

sections.title: Runner Security Best Practices
paragraphs: Security is where many teams underestimate the impact of runner design. A runner can see repository code, job logs, variables, artifacts, and possibly deployment credentials. Treat runners as trusted infrastructure, not disposable trivia.

Shared runners are convenient, but they are not ideal for highly sensitive production credentials. Even when GitLab isolates jobs, a broad shared environment increases your risk surface. For production deployments, it is safer to use self-hosted runners that you control, ideally scoped to one group or one project and protected by tags.
A protected runner only executes jobs from protected branches or protected tags. This prevents an untrusted feature branch from using a runner that has access to sensitive environments.
A protected variable is only exposed to jobs running on protected refs. This pairs naturally with protected runners.
That combination is far safer than placing production credentials in jobs that can run on any shared runner.

sections.title: Runner Concurrency Settings

sections.title: Final Takeaway
paragraphs: A GitLab Runner is the engine that turns CI/CD configuration into actual execution. Once you understand runner scope, executor types, tags, registration, and security boundaries, your pipelines become much easier to design and troubleshoot. For most teams, the Docker executor is the best starting point because it offers clean isolation, reproducible jobs, and excellent compatibility with modern CI workflows. As your platform grows, group runners, protected runners, and carefully chosen concurrency settings help you scale without losing control.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is a GitLab Runner?

It is the agent that actually executes your jobs. GitLab itself only orchestrates. It decides which jobs should run and in what order, then hands each one to a runner, which creates the environment, runs the script and streams the log back. Without at least one available runner, pipelines are created but every job sits pending forever. Runners can be shared across an instance, assigned to a group, or dedicated to a single project.
What is the difference between the runner executors?

The executor decides where a job's script runs. docker starts a fresh container per job from the image the job specifies, which gives clean isolation and is the usual choice. shell runs commands directly on the runner host, which is simple but leaves state behind between jobs and is a security concern on shared runners. kubernetes schedules each job as a Pod, which suits teams already running a cluster. docker-machine for autoscaling on cloud VMs is deprecated in favour of the newer autoscaling approach.
Why are my jobs stuck in pending?

No runner matches the job. The usual causes are a tags: value in the job that no registered runner carries, shared runners being disabled for the project, all runners being busy at their concurrency limit, or the runner being offline. The job page states which applies. Tag mismatches are the most common by a distance. Tags are exact-match strings, and a job tagged docker-builder will never run on a runner registered as docker_builder.
How do I install and register a runner?

Install the package from GitLab's repository for your distribution, then run gitlab-runner register and supply the GitLab URL, a registration token from the project or group's CI/CD settings, an executor, and a default image if using Docker. Registration writes an entry into config.toml, which is where you later adjust concurrency, volumes and cache settings. Modern GitLab uses runner authentication tokens created in the UI rather than the older shared registration token, so follow the flow your version presents.
What does concurrent in config.toml control?

The total number of jobs the runner process will execute simultaneously across all its registered runners. It is a global setting at the top of config.toml, separate from the per-runner limit. The default of 1 means jobs queue one at a time, which surprises teams who add a powerful machine and see no throughput improvement. Raise it to something the host can genuinely support. Bearing in mind each concurrent Docker job needs its own CPU, memory and disk for the image and build directory.
Are self-hosted runners safe to share between projects?

Only with care. A runner using the shell executor gives every job full access to the host, so any project that can run jobs on it can read files, credentials and other projects' build directories. The docker executor is much better isolated, but privileged mode, often enabled to allow Docker-in-Docker image builds, effectively grants root on the host and undoes that isolation. For untrusted code, or for repositories that accept outside contributions, use ephemeral runners that are destroyed after each job.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Control exactly when GitLab CI jobs run with rules:if, rules:changes and rules:exists, plus workflow rules, merge request pipelines and manual jobs.

One of the fastest ways to waste CI minutes is to run every GitLab job on every push, tag, merge request, and schedule. That noisy approach might look simple at first, but it scales poorly. Frontend tests run even when only backend files changed. Production deployment jobs appear in feature branch pipelines where they can never be used. Documentation-only commits trigger expensive integration suites. Teams start ignoring red pipelines because too much irrelevant automation is running.

That is why GitLab CI rules matter. Rules let you decide when a job should run, when it should be manual, when it should be skipped, and even when the entire pipeline should exist. Once you learn GitLab CI rules if, GitLab CI rules changes, GitLab CI rules exists, and workflow:rules, you can build pipelines that are cheaper, faster, and much easier to understand.

sections.title: Why Controlling When Jobs Run Matters
paragraphs: A well-designed pipeline should create signal, not noise. Job conditions matter because they help you:

For example, a monorepo may contain frontend, backend, infrastructure, and docs directories. If a docs change triggers the full stack every time, the pipeline becomes slow and expensive. With rules, you can make GitLab intelligent enough to run only the required jobs.

sections.title: rules vs the Older only/except
paragraphs: Historically, GitLab pipelines used only and except to decide whether jobs should run. That syntax still appears in older tutorials, but rules is the modern and more flexible approach.
This is simple, but limited. Once you want branch conditions, merge request logic, file change checks, manual behavior, and failure handling in one place, only/except becomes awkward.
With rules, each rule item can combine conditions and behaviors such as if, changes, exists, when, and allow_failure. That makes pipeline logic much more expressive.

codeBlock.code:
deploy-prod:
  script: ./deploy.sh
  only:
    - main

sections.title: rules:if for Variable-Based Conditions
paragraphs: The most common rule type is rules:if, which evaluates a condition using CI/CD variables.
A simple example that runs only on the main branch:
If the expression is true, the job is included. If no rule matches, the job is skipped unless you add a catch-all rule.
You will use a few predefined variables frequently:
These variables let you describe most GitLab pipeline trigger conditions.
Here, the rule matches when CI_MERGE_REQUEST_ID exists. This is a concise way to create a GitLab CI merge request pipeline job.
This pattern says: if the pipeline is for a tag, never run the job; otherwise run it normally.
This is useful when the same repository supports push pipelines, scheduled pipelines, API-triggered pipelines, and merge request pipelines.

codeBlock.code:
unit-tests:
  script: npm test
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"'

sections.title: rules:changes for File-Based Execution
paragraphs: Sometimes you do not care which branch changed. You care what files changed. That is what rules:changes is for.
Suppose you have a frontend directory and only want frontend tests when frontend code changes.
This is one of the most valuable optimizations in a monorepo. It makes GitLab CI rules changes a powerful cost-control feature.
Other good use cases include:
That job now runs when backend code or Python dependencies change.

codeBlock.code:
frontend-tests:
  script:
    - cd frontend
    - npm ci
    - npm test
  rules:
    - changes:
        - frontend/**/*

sections.title: rules:exists for Repository-Aware Jobs
paragraphs: The third major condition type is rules:exists. This tells GitLab to include a job only if specific files are present in the repository.
This is useful for reusable templates or shared CI configuration. You might include a generic job in many repositories, but only want it to activate when the repo actually contains certain files.
rules:exists is especially helpful in platform engineering, where one central CI template serves many project types.

codeBlock.code:
docker-build:
  script: docker build -t myapp .
  rules:
    - exists:
        - Dockerfile

sections.title: rules:when and Job Behavior
paragraphs: A rule does not just decide whether a job is created. It can also decide how that job behaves through rules:when.
This is common when you want a deploy button to appear, but you do not want GitLab to deploy automatically.
That job is useful for diagnostics after a failing build or test stage.
Delayed jobs are less common, but helpful for staged rollouts or post-deploy checks.

codeBlock.code:
deploy-staging:
  script: ./deploy-staging.sh
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"'
      when: manual

sections.title: rules:allow_failure
paragraphs: Some jobs are informative but should not block the whole pipeline. For those, you can combine rules with allow_failure.
If this job fails, the pipeline still succeeds. That is useful for optional quality checks, early-stage security scanning, or experimental tooling.

codeBlock.code:
experimental-scan:
  script: ./experimental-check.sh
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"'
      allow_failure: true

sections.title: Manual Jobs with when: manual and allow_failure: true
paragraphs: A very common pattern is a manual action that should not mark the pipeline as failed if nobody clicks it.
Teams often use this for review apps, ad hoc preview deployments, or optional extra checks.

codeBlock.code:
deploy-preview:
  script: ./deploy-preview.sh
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_ID'
      when: manual
      allow_failure: true

sections.title: Combining Multiple Rules
paragraphs: Understanding how multiple rule items are evaluated is essential.
Each item in the rules: list is evaluated from top to bottom. The first matching item decides the outcome. In practice, this means the list behaves like OR logic between items.
This job runs if the branch is main or if the pipeline is a merge request pipeline.
Within a single rule item, conditions combine together. If you place if and changes in the same item, both must match.
This job runs only when the pipeline is a merge request pipeline and frontend files changed.
Because the first matching rule wins, put the most specific exclusions first.

codeBlock.code:
job:
  script: echo hello
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"'
    - if: '$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_ID'

sections.title: Merge Request Pipelines vs Branch Pipelines
paragraphs: A common source of confusion is duplicate pipelines. If a push to a branch that has an open merge request creates both a branch pipeline and a merge request pipeline, your jobs may run twice.
Why does this happen? GitLab can create pipelines for different sources:
If your rules do not distinguish these sources, duplicate or noisy execution is easy to create.
A typical strategy is:
This job runs in merge request pipelines and on main branch pipelines, but not on every feature branch push.

codeBlock.code:
lint:
  script: npm run lint
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"'
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"'

sections.title: workflow:rules for Controlling the Entire Pipeline
paragraphs: Job-level rules are powerful, but sometimes you want to stop an entire pipeline from being created. That is where workflow:rules comes in.

This is one of the best ways to avoid unnecessary feature branch pipelines and duplicate execution. It lets you centralize high-level pipeline creation logic before job-level rules are even considered.

codeBlock.code:
workflow:
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"'
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"'
    - when: never

sections.title: Complete Practical Example: MR vs Main Branch
paragraphs: Here is a realistic .gitlab-ci.yml example that behaves differently for merge requests and for the main branch.
This is a strong pattern because it keeps merge request pipelines focused on validation and keeps main branch pipelines ready for release.

codeBlock.code:
workflow:
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"'
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"'
    - when: never

stages:
  - lint
  - test
  - build
  - deploy

lint:
  stage: lint
  image: node:20
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm run lint
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"'
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"'

frontend-tests:
  stage: test
  image: node:20
  script:
    - cd frontend
    - npm ci
    - npm test
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"'
      changes:
        - frontend/**/*
        - package-lock.json
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"'

build-app:
  stage: build
  image: node:20
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm run build
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"'

preview-deploy:
  stage: deploy
  script: ./deploy-preview.sh
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"'
      when: manual
      allow_failure: true

production-deploy:
  stage: deploy
  script: ./deploy-prod.sh
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"'
      when: manual

sections.title: Final Takeaway
paragraphs: GitLab pipeline rules are not just syntax trivia. They are how you turn a pipeline from a blunt instrument into a precise automation system. Use rules:if for branch, tag, and pipeline-source logic. Use rules:changes to save CI minutes in monorepos. Use rules:exists for reusable templates. Use when, manual, and allow_failure to shape job behavior. And when you need to decide whether a pipeline should exist at all, reach for workflow:rules.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How do rules work in GitLab CI?

Each job's rules: list is evaluated top to bottom and the first matching rule wins. Evaluation stops there, and later rules are never considered. The matched rule determines whether the job is added to the pipeline and with what when, allow_failure and variables. If no rule matches, the job is excluded from the pipeline entirely rather than failing. Because of the first-match behaviour, ordering rules from most specific to most general is essential; a broad catch-all placed first makes everything below it dead code.
Why is my job not appearing in the pipeline?

No rule matched, so the job was never created. This looks different from a failure. The job is absent from the pipeline graph rather than shown as skipped or failed. The most frequent cause is a branch condition that does not apply to the pipeline type: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH is not set in merge request pipelines, so a rule written against it silently never matches there. Use $CI_MERGE_REQUEST_SOURCE_BRANCH_NAME or a $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event" condition for those.
What is the difference between rules:if and rules:changes?

if evaluates an expression against CI/CD variables: the branch name, the pipeline source, a custom variable. changes matches when specific files were modified in the commit, which is how you run a job only when the relevant part of a monorepo changed. They can be combined in a single rule, and both must be satisfied for it to match. A caution with changes: on pipelines where GitLab cannot compute a meaningful diff, such as the first pipeline on a new branch, it can evaluate as true and run jobs you expected to be skipped.
How do I stop duplicate pipelines running for branches and merge requests?

This happens when a project has both branch pipelines and merge request pipelines enabled without rules that distinguish them, so each push creates two. The standard fix is workflow-level rules that run a merge request pipeline when one exists, run a branch pipeline only when no merge request is open for that branch, and always run on the default branch. Putting this in a top-level workflow: rules: block applies it to the whole pipeline rather than repeating the logic on every job.
What does when: never do?

It excludes the job when that rule matches, which is how you carve exceptions out of a broader condition. A common pattern is a first rule with when: never for the cases you want to skip, draft merge requests, documentation-only changes, followed by a general rule that runs the job otherwise. Because evaluation stops at the first match, the exclusion must come before the rule it is excepting from, which is the most frequent mistake with this keyword.
Can I use rules and only/except in the same job?

No. GitLab rejects the pipeline with a configuration error if a job contains both. They are alternative mechanisms, and rules is the current one, only and except still work for backwards compatibility but receive no new features. When migrating, do it a whole job at a time rather than mixing, and remember that rules defaults differ: a job with rules and no matching entry is not created at all, where only had a more permissive default.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Track deployments with GitLab CI environments: the environment keyword, static versus dynamic environments, review apps, protected environments and approvals.

In GitLab CI/CD, an environment is not just a label you attach to a deployment job. It is a first-class deployment tracking concept that helps GitLab understand where your application was deployed, when it was deployed, which job performed the deployment, and which commit reached that target. If you treat environments seriously, GitLab becomes more than a build runner. It becomes a deployment history system, a release visibility system, and a foundation for safer delivery.

That is why topics like GitLab CI environments, GitLab environment tracking, GitLab review apps, GitLab protected environments, and GitLab deployment approval matter so much in modern DevOps workflows.

sections.title: What Are GitLab Environments?
paragraphs: A GitLab environment represents a deployment target such as:

When a CI job declares an environment, GitLab records the deployment and links it to the commit, pipeline, job, and, when available, a URL. This gives your team a clear answer to operational questions such as:
This is the reason GitLab environments are about deployment tracking, not only syntax.

sections.title: The environment Keyword in Jobs
paragraphs: You define environments using the environment keyword inside a job.
This does two things:
The name field identifies the environment. Static names such as dev, staging, and production are common for long-lived environments.

The url field improves usability. Instead of making teammates search for the deployed site, GitLab can display a direct environment link. This is especially helpful for QA, product managers, and reviewers.

codeBlock.code:
deploy-staging:
  stage: deploy
  script:
    - ./deploy-staging.sh
  environment:
    name: staging
    url: https://staging.example.com

sections.title: Static vs Dynamic Environments
paragraphs: A big part of understanding GitLab CI deployment environments is recognizing that not all environments are permanent.
A static environment is long-lived and reused over time. Examples include:
These environments usually represent stable infrastructure targets and receive repeated deployments.
A dynamic environment is created temporarily, often for a branch or merge request, and then removed when no longer needed.
Dynamic environments are the foundation of GitLab review apps, which create per-merge-request previews that reviewers can click and test.

sections.title: Viewing Deployment History in GitLab
paragraphs: One of the best benefits of environment tracking is visibility in the GitLab UI. Once jobs declare environments, GitLab can show:
This makes release troubleshooting much easier. If someone asks, “What commit is in staging right now?” you do not need to dig through Slack or guess from timestamps. GitLab already knows.
For regulated or fast-moving teams, this audit trail is extremely valuable because deployment information stays close to the source code and pipeline that produced it.

sections.title: Dynamic Environments for Merge Requests
paragraphs: Dynamic environments become especially powerful in merge request workflows. A common pattern is to create a unique environment name using the merge request IID.
This means each merge request gets its own preview environment, such as:
That preview can be linked directly in the merge request, making it easy for reviewers to test behavior without checking out code locally.

codeBlock.code:
review-app:
  stage: deploy
  script:
    - ./deploy-review.sh
  environment:
    name: review/$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID
    url: https://review-$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID.example.com

sections.title: Review Apps in GitLab CI/CD
paragraphs: GitLab review apps are one of the most developer-friendly features in GitLab CI. Instead of reviewing screenshots or abstract descriptions, product and QA teams can interact with a live deployment created just for the merge request.
A review app usually includes:
The experience becomes even better when the environment URL is automatically posted into the merge request widget.

sections.title: The on_stop Keyword and Stop Job Pattern
paragraphs: Dynamic environments should not live forever. Cloud resources cost money, and stale review environments create confusion. GitLab solves this with the on_stop keyword and a paired stop job.
This pattern tells GitLab which job stops the environment. In many teams, the stop job is triggered manually, automatically on merge, or via cleanup policies depending on the platform.
The important point is conceptual: creating a dynamic environment should always come with a cleanup strategy.

codeBlock.code:
review-app:
  stage: deploy
  script:
    - ./deploy-review.sh
  environment:
    name: review/$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID
    url: https://review-$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID.example.com
    on_stop: stop-review-app

sections.title: Protected Environments and Deployment Approvals
paragraphs: Production is different from development. Most organizations do not want any successful pipeline to push straight to production. That is where GitLab protected environments come in.
A protected environment lets you restrict who can deploy to a specific target such as production. Depending on your GitLab tier and settings, you can require:
This creates a stronger governance layer around GitLab deployment approval workflows.

Each layer reduces the chance of an unsafe production release.

sections.title: Deployment Frequency and DORA Metrics
paragraphs: GitLab environments also support measurement. Because GitLab can track deployments to environments, it can contribute to metrics such as deployment frequency, one of the DORA metrics widely used to evaluate software delivery performance.
DORA metrics often include:

When your pipeline accurately records deployments to real environments, GitLab can provide better operational insight. This is another reason to model environments explicitly instead of treating deployments as anonymous scripts.
If your organization wants to improve release speed without sacrificing stability, proper environment tracking is a foundational step.

sections.title: Environment-Scoped Variables
paragraphs: Another powerful feature is environment scoped variables. Sometimes the same application uses different values depending on where it is deployed:
Instead of hardcoding separate jobs for every small variation, you can define variables in GitLab settings and scope them to specific environments.
Then the same deployment logic can run across multiple targets while GitLab injects the correct value for the current environment.
This reduces duplication and helps keep sensitive configuration out of the repository.

paragraphs: Here is a complete example showing environment tracking across a simple delivery flow.

  rules:
    - if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"'
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"'

stages:

  - deploy

unit-tests:
  stage: test
  image: node:20

    - npm test

review-app:
  stage: deploy

    - ./scripts/deploy-review.sh
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"'
  environment:
    name: review/$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID
    url: https://review-$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID.example.com
    on_stop: stop-review-app

stop-review-app:
  stage: deploy
  script:
    - ./scripts/destroy-review.sh
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"'
      when: manual
      allow_failure: true
  environment:
    name: review/$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID
    action: stop

deploy-dev:
  stage: deploy
  script:
    - ./scripts/deploy-dev.sh
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"'
  environment:
    name: development
    url: https://dev.example.com

deploy-staging:
  stage: deploy
  script:
    - ./scripts/deploy-staging.sh
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"'
      when: manual
  environment:
    name: staging
    url: https://staging.example.com

deploy-production:
  stage: deploy
  script:
    - ./scripts/deploy-production.sh
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"'
      when: manual
  environment:
    name: production
    url: https://app.example.com

sections.title: Final Takeaway
paragraphs: GitLab environments are one of the features that turn a basic CI pipeline into a real delivery platform. By using the environment keyword, setting URLs, modeling static and dynamic targets, adding review apps, wiring stop jobs with on_stop, protecting production, and scoping variables per environment, you gain far more than deployment automation. You gain visibility, safer releases, better collaboration, and stronger operational insight.

sections.title: Knowledge Check
paragraphs: What is the main value of a GitLab environment beyond simply labeling a job?
Why is the on_stop pattern important for dynamic review app environments?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is a GitLab environment and why do I need one?

An environment is a named deployment target, staging, production, or a per-branch review app, that GitLab tracks over time. Adding an environment: key to a deploy job gives you a deployment history showing what was deployed where and by whom, a link straight to the running application, the ability to protect the target so only certain people can deploy to it, environment-scoped variables, and the data behind DORA metrics. Without it a deploy job is just a script and none of that exists.
What is the difference between a static and a dynamic environment?

A static environment has a fixed name, such as production, and is deployed to repeatedly. A dynamic environment has a name built from CI variables, typically review/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG, so every branch gets its own. Dynamic environments are how review apps work: each merge request deploys a live copy reviewers can click through. Because they are created per branch, they need an on_stop job to tear them down or they accumulate indefinitely.
How do I clean up review apps automatically?

Pair the deploy job with a stop job and reference it via environment: on_stop:. GitLab runs the stop job when the branch is deleted or the merge request is merged or closed, which is what destroys the deployed resources. Setting auto_stop_in adds a time-based expiry as a safety net, auto_stop_in: 1 week stops environments that were forgotten. Without both, abandoned review apps keep consuming infrastructure and cost money quietly.
How do I require approval before deploying to production?

Use a protected environment. In the project's CI/CD settings, protect the production environment and specify which users or groups are allowed to deploy to it, optionally requiring a number of approvals before the job runs. This is enforced by GitLab rather than by convention, so an ordinary contributor cannot deploy even by editing the pipeline. Combining it with when: manual on the job gives you both an explicit gate and an authorisation check.
What are environment-scoped variables?

CI/CD variables can be limited to a specific environment, so DATABASE_URL resolves to different values in staging and production while the pipeline uses one variable name. The job receives the value matching the environment it declares. This removes the need for branching logic or separately named variables per environment, and it keeps production credentials out of jobs that deploy anywhere else.
Do environments cost anything or affect DORA metrics?

Environments themselves are a free GitLab feature; you only pay for the infrastructure you deploy to. They are also what makes DORA metrics work. Deployment frequency and lead time for changes are both derived from deployments recorded against environments, so a team that deploys without declaring an environment will see those metrics stay empty regardless of how often they actually ship.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Build and push Docker images in GitLab CI: compare Docker-in-Docker with Kaniko, authenticate to the Container Registry, pick tags and follow a full example.

Docker and GitLab CI/CD are a natural pair. GitLab jobs often run inside containers, and many delivery workflows also need to build Docker images, tag them, and push them to a registry. That creates two related but different concepts that beginners sometimes confuse:

Understanding both is crucial if you want to design reliable GitLab CI Docker pipelines. This tutorial explains how the image keyword works, how to build and push images, why Docker-in-Docker exists, when it is risky, when Kaniko is a better alternative, and how to authenticate to the GitLab Container Registry and Docker Hub.

sections.title: Using Docker Images in CI Jobs with image
paragraphs: The simplest Docker feature in GitLab CI is the image keyword. It tells GitLab which container image to use as the runtime environment for a job.
In this example, the job itself runs inside the node:20 image. That means Node.js and npm are already available in the execution environment.
This pattern is ideal because it avoids installing language runtimes by hand during every pipeline run. Instead, the job starts from a purpose-built container image.
Different jobs often need different tools:
By selecting the right image per job, you keep pipelines clean, reproducible, and easier to maintain.

codeBlock.code:
lint:
  image: node:20
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm run lint

sections.title: Global Default Image vs Per-Job Image
paragraphs: GitLab lets you define an image globally or on individual jobs.
This is convenient when most jobs use the same runtime.
Use a per-job image when a specific job needs different tooling. This keeps each job minimal and precise.
This design is common in mature GitLab CI Dockerfile workflows because it reduces repetition without sacrificing clarity.

codeBlock.code:
default:
  image: node:20

build:
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm run build

test:
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm test

sections.title: Pulling Images from Docker Hub, GitLab Container Registry, and Private Registries
paragraphs: The image keyword can point to multiple registry sources.
This is the default experience most developers know.
This is useful when your team publishes internal base images, such as a hardened Node.js image with preinstalled tools.

You can also pull from private registries if the runner or job has permission. Depending on your setup, that may involve runner-level Docker authentication, predefined variables, or cloud-specific registry login steps.
For enterprise DevOps teams, internal base images are often the best practice because they centralize patching, security hardening, and tool standardization.

codeBlock.code: image: python:3.12

sections.title: Building a Docker Image in CI: The Real Challenge
paragraphs: Running a job inside a Docker image is easy. Building a new Docker image in that job is trickier.
Why? Because docker build expects access to a Docker daemon. If your GitLab job already runs in a container, it does not automatically have a Docker daemon inside it.
That is the core challenge behind GitLab CI build Docker image pipelines: Docker usually needs Docker.
This leads to the classic Docker-in-Docker pattern.

sections.title: Docker-in-Docker (DinD): How It Works
paragraphs: Docker-in-Docker, often called DinD or dind GitLab, means your CI job talks to a separate Docker daemon running as a service container.
A standard GitLab example looks like this:
Now the job container can execute docker build, docker tag, and docker push against the daemon in the service container.

codeBlock.code:
build-image:
  image: docker:27
  services:
    - docker:27-dind
  variables:
    DOCKER_HOST: tcp://docker:2375
    DOCKER_TLS_CERTDIR: ""
  script:
    - docker version
    - docker build -t myapp:$CI_COMMIT_SHA .

sections.title: Why DinD Is Popular
paragraphs: DinD remains common because it is familiar. Many developers already know local Docker commands, so reusing them in CI feels natural. It supports a wide range of image build tasks, including:
For many teams, especially those starting with GitLab CI Docker build push workflows, DinD is the first solution they learn.

sections.title: Security Concerns with Docker-in-Docker
paragraphs: DinD is useful, but it is not always the safest choice. Many DinD setups require privileged mode on the runner. Privileged mode grants broad kernel capabilities and weakens isolation.
Why is that concerning?
This does not mean DinD is always wrong. It means you should use it deliberately.
Consider alternatives when:
That is where Kaniko becomes attractive.

sections.title: Kaniko as a DinD Alternative
paragraphs: Kaniko is a tool designed to build container images from a Dockerfile without requiring a Docker daemon. That makes it a strong option for GitLab CI Kaniko pipelines.
A basic Kaniko job looks like this:
If your main goal is just to build and push images securely, Kaniko is often a strong fit.

codeBlock.code:
build-image-kaniko:
  image:
    name: gcr.io/kaniko-project/executor:latest
    entrypoint: [""]
  script:
    - mkdir -p /kaniko/.docker
    - echo '{"auths":{"'$CI_REGISTRY'":{"username":"'$CI_REGISTRY_USER'","password":"'$CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD'"}}}' > /kaniko/.docker/config.json
    - /kaniko/executor --context "$CI_PROJECT_DIR" --dockerfile "$CI_PROJECT_DIR/Dockerfile" --destination "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA"

sections.title: Pushing to GitLab Container Registry
paragraphs: The GitLab Container Registry integrates naturally with GitLab CI/CD. GitLab exposes predefined variables such as:
These make GitLab CI push Docker image workflows straightforward.
This works especially well when your source code and image destination both live in GitLab.

codeBlock.code:
script:
  - echo "$CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD" | docker login -u "$CI_REGISTRY_USER" --password-stdin "$CI_REGISTRY"
  - docker build -t "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA" .
  - docker push "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA"

sections.title: Pushing to Docker Hub
paragraphs: You may also need to push to Docker Hub. In that case, store your credentials as masked CI/CD variables such as:
Then authenticate during the job:

codeBlock.code:
script:
  - echo "$DOCKERHUB_PASSWORD" | docker login -u "$DOCKERHUB_USERNAME" --password-stdin
  - docker build -t myorg/myapp:$CI_COMMIT_SHA .
  - docker push myorg/myapp:$CI_COMMIT_SHA

sections.title: Tagging Strategies for Docker Images in GitLab CI
paragraphs: Good image tags make releases traceable and predictable. A few common strategies are especially useful.
This is the most traceable tag because it points to an exact commit.
This is ideal for versioned releases such as v1.4.0.
This is convenient, but should not be your only tag because latest is mutable and less auditable.
In many real pipelines, push more than one tag:
This gives you both usability and traceability.

codeBlock.code: docker build -t "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA" .

sections.title: Multi-Stage Builds and --target
paragraphs: If your Dockerfile uses multi-stage builds, GitLab CI can build specific stages with --target.
In CI, you might build only the intermediate stage for testing or caching purposes:
Or build the full runtime image for publication:
This is useful when your pipeline separates validation from release packaging.

codeBlock.code:
FROM node:20 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM nginx:alpine AS runtime
COPY --from=build /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html

sections.title: Complete Working Example: Build, Tag, and Push to GitLab Container Registry
paragraphs: Here is a full GitLab CI Docker build push example using DinD.
This is a practical, production-style starting point for many teams.

codeBlock.code:
stages:
  - test
  - build

default:
  image: node:20

unit-tests:
  stage: test
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm test

build-and-push-image:
  stage: build
  image: docker:27
  services:
    - docker:27-dind
  variables:
    DOCKER_HOST: tcp://docker:2375
    DOCKER_TLS_CERTDIR: ""
  before_script:
    - echo "$CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD" | docker login -u "$CI_REGISTRY_USER" --password-stdin "$CI_REGISTRY"
  script:
    - docker build -t "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA" -t "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:latest" .
    - docker push "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA"
    - docker push "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:latest"
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"'

paragraphs: If you want to avoid privileged DinD, here is a concise Kaniko version:
This is often easier to justify in security-conscious environments.

  stage: build

    name: gcr.io/kaniko-project/executor:latest
    entrypoint: [""]

    - mkdir -p /kaniko/.docker
    - echo '{"auths":{"'$CI_REGISTRY'":{"username":"'$CI_REGISTRY_USER'","password":"'$CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD'"}}}' > /kaniko/.docker/config.json
    - /kaniko/executor         --context "$CI_PROJECT_DIR"         --dockerfile "$CI_PROJECT_DIR/Dockerfile"         --destination "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA"         --destination "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:latest"
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"'

sections.title: Final Takeaway
paragraphs: GitLab CI and Docker work beautifully together when you separate the concerns clearly. Use the image keyword to choose the right runtime for each job. Use DinD when you need a familiar Docker CLI workflow and accept the security implications. Use Kaniko when you want a daemonless image build approach. Authenticate safely to the GitLab Container Registry or Docker Hub with CI variables, tag images in a traceable way, and keep your Docker pipelines honest by testing before you publish.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How do I build a Docker image inside a GitLab CI job?

A CI job already runs inside a container, so there is no Docker daemon available by default and docker build fails with "Cannot connect to the Docker daemon". The two established approaches are Docker-in-Docker, where you attach a docker:dind service that provides a daemon for the job, and Kaniko, which builds images from a Dockerfile without needing a daemon at all. DinD is more familiar and requires privileged mode; Kaniko avoids that and is the safer option on shared runners.
What is Docker-in-Docker and why is it a security concern?

DinD runs a Docker daemon as a service container alongside your job so the job can issue docker build and docker push. It requires the runner to be configured with privileged = true, and a privileged container can access the host's devices and kernel capabilities, which effectively means any job on that runner can take over the machine. On a runner dedicated to trusted code this may be acceptable; on a shared runner, or any project accepting merge requests from forks, it is a serious risk.
What is Kaniko and when should I use it?

Kaniko builds container images from a Dockerfile inside a container, in userspace, with no Docker daemon and no privileged mode. It is the right default on shared or multi-tenant runners precisely because it removes the privilege escalation path that DinD opens. The trade-offs are that its caching behaviour differs from Docker's and a few exotic Dockerfile features are unsupported, so an existing DinD pipeline occasionally needs small adjustments when migrating.
How do I push an image to the GitLab Container Registry?

GitLab provides predefined variables for this. The registry address, and a per-job token and username that authorise the push without you creating any credentials. Log in with those, tag the image using the registry image path variable, and push. Because the token is scoped to the job and expires with it, this is considerably safer than storing a long-lived registry password in CI/CD variables, and it needs no setup beyond enabling the registry on the project.
How should I tag images built in CI?

Tag with something that traces back to exact source. The commit SHA is the standard choice, and GitLab supplies it as a predefined variable. Deploy that immutable tag rather than a moving one, so a rollback has a specific image to return to and an incident timeline can be reconstructed. It is common to additionally push a moving tag such as the branch name or latest for convenience, but nothing should be deployed by those, since two deploys of the same moving tag can run different code.
Why does my job fail with "Cannot connect to the Docker daemon"?

Because nothing is providing one. Either add the docker:dind service and the environment variables that point the client at it, or switch to Kaniko, which does not need a daemon. A subtler variant of this error occurs when DinD is configured but the runner is not in privileged mode. The service container fails to start, and the job's error looks identical even though the cause is the runner configuration rather than the pipeline.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Run tests in GitLab CI: collect JUnit reports, view results in merge requests, extract coverage with a regex, run in parallel and follow a Jest pipeline.

Automated testing is not a “nice to have” in CI/CD. It is the control system that tells you whether a change is safe to merge, safe to release, and safe to trust. Without automated tests in your pipeline, every merge becomes a guess and every deployment becomes a gamble. That is why GitLab CI testing, GitLab CI unit tests, GitLab CI test reports, and GitLab CI code coverage are core skills for any DevOps engineer or software team.

In GitLab, testing is not just about running a command and getting a pass or fail result. GitLab can also capture structured JUnit XML reports, display test summaries in merge requests, extract coverage percentages from logs, visualize line-level coverage changes, publish badges, and even parallelize test execution to keep feedback fast.

sections.title: Why Automated Testing in CI Is Non-Negotiable
paragraphs: Local testing is helpful, but it is not enough. Developers have different operating systems, tool versions, environment variables, and local habits. CI gives you one consistent place where every important change is validated the same way.
Automated testing in GitLab CI matters because it helps you:
A pipeline without testing may still look automated, but it is missing a key safety layer.

sections.title: Running Unit Tests in a GitLab CI Job
paragraphs: At its simplest, a test job is just a normal CI job that runs your test command.
This is the foundational pattern for GitLab CI Jest pipelines.
This is the starting point for GitLab CI pytest workflows.
The language does not matter as much as the principle: every push or merge request should run the relevant automated tests in a clean environment.

codeBlock.code:
unit-tests:
  stage: test
  image: node:20
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm test

sections.title: Collecting JUnit XML Reports
paragraphs: A plain pass or fail result is useful, but GitLab can do much more when you upload test results in JUnit XML format. This is done with artifacts:reports:junit.
When GitLab understands your test results as structured data, it can:
This is one of the most valuable upgrades from “basic CI” to “developer-friendly CI.”
If tests fail, you usually still want the JUnit report. Setting when: always ensures GitLab uploads the report even when the job exits with a non-zero status.

codeBlock.code:
unit-tests:
  stage: test
  image: node:20
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm test -- --ci --reporters=default --reporters=jest-junit
  artifacts:
    when: always
    reports:
      junit: junit.xml

sections.title: Viewing Test Results in the Merge Request UI
paragraphs: After you upload a GitLab CI JUnit report, GitLab can display a test summary widget in the merge request UI. Reviewers can often see:
This shortens feedback loops dramatically. Instead of opening raw job logs and scrolling for minutes, developers get structured information in the place where code review already happens.
For busy teams, this alone is a huge quality-of-life improvement.

sections.title: Code Coverage: What It Measures
paragraphs: Code coverage describes how much of your application code is exercised by your tests. It is usually expressed as a percentage.
Coverage can be measured in different ways, such as:
In GitLab CI, the most common beginner use case is to extract a coverage percentage from test output and show it in the pipeline or merge request.
Coverage is not the same as quality. High coverage does not automatically mean good tests. But low or absent coverage is often a warning sign that important paths are untested.

sections.title: Extracting Coverage Percentage with coverage Regex
paragraphs: GitLab can parse a percentage from the job log using the coverage keyword.
This tells GitLab to look for a matching percentage in the output.
Different test tools print coverage in different formats. GitLab therefore lets you provide a regex suited to your tool.
The point is not the exact regex syntax. The point is to make the percentage visible in GitLab so coverage becomes part of daily development.

codeBlock.code:
unit-tests:
  stage: test
  image: node:20
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm test -- --coverage
  coverage: '/All files[^|]*\|[^|]*\s+([0-9]+\.?[0-9]*)%/'

sections.title: Coverage Visualization in Merge Request Diffs
paragraphs: A single total percentage is useful, but line-level visualization is even better. GitLab supports coverage visualization in merge requests using report formats such as Cobertura.
That usually looks like this:
With a proper coverage report, GitLab can highlight covered and uncovered lines directly in the MR diff. This helps reviewers answer a practical question: did the new code actually get tested?
That is much more actionable than a single percentage alone.

codeBlock.code:
artifacts:
  reports:
    coverage_report:
      coverage_format: cobertura
      path: coverage/cobertura-coverage.xml

sections.title: Coverage Badges for README Files
paragraphs: Many teams like to display a GitLab CI coverage badge in their README. A badge makes test status and coverage visible at a glance.
Badges should not become vanity metrics, but they can be a useful indicator when backed by real testing discipline.

sections.title: Failing the Pipeline on Coverage Drop
paragraphs: Sometimes you want more than reporting. You want enforcement. One way is to make your test tool fail when coverage falls below a threshold.
Jest supports coverage thresholds directly in configuration, such as package.json or jest.config.js.
If the actual coverage falls below the threshold, the test job fails and the pipeline turns red.
A visible metric is helpful. An enforced quality gate is stronger. Coverage thresholds prevent silent erosion over time.
That said, teams should choose realistic thresholds. Arbitrary numbers can encourage meaningless tests written only to satisfy the metric.

sections.title: Parallel Test Execution with parallel
paragraphs: As projects grow, tests get slower. One way to improve feedback speed is parallel execution.
GitLab supports the parallel keyword:
This creates multiple job instances. To use it well, your test framework or wrapper script should know how to shard or distribute the tests across those parallel jobs.
Parallelization helps when:
Keep in mind that parallel jobs may increase CI usage even while reducing wall-clock time.

codeBlock.code:
unit-tests:
  stage: test
  image: node:20
  parallel: 4
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm test

sections.title: Test Environment Variables in CI
paragraphs: Tests often need configuration values such as:
You can define these in GitLab CI variables and use them safely in jobs.
For sensitive values, store them in Settings → CI/CD → Variables instead of hardcoding them in the YAML file.
This is especially important for integration tests that touch ephemeral databases, staging services, or external APIs.

codeBlock.code:
integration-tests:
  stage: test
  image: node:20
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm run test:integration
  variables:
    TEST_ENV: ci

sections.title: Complete Example: Node.js App with Jest, Coverage, and JUnit Artifacts
paragraphs: Here is a full example of a practical GitLab CI testing pipeline for a Node.js project.
This is a great baseline for many JavaScript projects.

codeBlock.code:
stages:
  - test

default:
  image: node:20

jest-tests:
  stage: test
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm test -- --ci --coverage --reporters=default --reporters=jest-junit
  variables:
    JEST_JUNIT_OUTPUT_FILE: junit.xml
    TEST_ENV: ci
  coverage: '/All files[^|]*\|[^|]*\s+([0-9]+\.?[0-9]*)%/'
  artifacts:
    when: always
    paths:
      - coverage/
      - junit.xml
    reports:
      junit: junit.xml
      coverage_report:
        coverage_format: cobertura
        path: coverage/cobertura-coverage.xml
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"'
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"'

sections.title: Example: Python with pytest and JUnit
paragraphs: For comparison, here is the same concept with Python.
The tools differ, but the GitLab pattern is the same: run tests, generate structured reports, upload them as artifacts, and let GitLab enrich the review experience.

codeBlock.code:
pytest-tests:
  stage: test
  image: python:3.12
  script:
    - pip install -r requirements.txt
    - pip install pytest pytest-cov junitxml
    - pytest --junitxml=junit.xml --cov=. --cov-report=xml:coverage/cobertura-coverage.xml
  artifacts:
    when: always
    reports:
      junit: junit.xml
      coverage_report:
        coverage_format: cobertura
        path: coverage/cobertura-coverage.xml

sections.title: Final Takeaway
paragraphs: GitLab testing features do more than turn a job green or red. They let you build fast, visible, enforceable quality gates. Start with straightforward unit test jobs. Then add JUnit reports so merge requests show structured failures. Add coverage extraction and Cobertura visualization so reviewers can see what changed. Use thresholds when your team is ready for stronger enforcement. And if the suite gets slow, scale it with parallel execution and better CI design.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How do I show test results in the GitLab merge request?

Have your test runner emit JUnit XML and declare it under artifacts: reports: junit:. GitLab parses the file and renders a test summary in the merge request showing which tests newly failed, which were fixed, and how long they took. Far more useful than reading a job log. Nearly every test framework can produce JUnit XML, usually through a reporter package or a command-line flag. Set artifacts: when: always so reports are still collected when the job fails, which is exactly when you need them.
How do I get a code coverage percentage into GitLab?

Set the coverage: keyword on the job to a regular expression that matches the coverage number in the job's output. GitLab extracts it and displays it on the pipeline, on the merge request, and in the coverage badge for your README. For per-line coverage highlighting in the merge request diff, additionally publish a Cobertura or equivalent report under artifacts: reports: coverage_report:, which is a separate mechanism from the percentage regex.
Should I fail the pipeline when coverage drops?

A threshold is useful but an absolute one is a blunt instrument. Teams either set it low enough to be meaningless or spend time writing tests to satisfy a number rather than to catch bugs. A more workable approach is to fail on a significant decrease relative to the target branch, which catches genuinely untested new code without penalising a refactor that removes well-covered lines. Whatever you choose, make it visible in the merge request so the conversation happens at review time.
How do I speed up a slow test suite in CI?

Use parallel: to split the job into several instances that run simultaneously, with your test runner sharding by the index variables GitLab provides. Cache dependencies so installation is not repeated on every run. Split fast unit tests from slow integration tests into separate stages so the quick feedback arrives first and the pipeline fails early. If a suite is slow because of genuinely slow tests rather than volume, parallelism only hides the cost. The individual tests still need attention.
Why do my tests pass locally but fail in CI?

Almost always environment differences. CI starts from a clean container with no leftover state, so tests that depend on a previously seeded database, a file written by an earlier run, or a locally installed tool will fail. Tests that assume a particular execution order also break under parallelism. Timezone and locale differ from a developer laptop surprisingly often. Reproduce it by running the same image locally with the same command the job uses, which usually surfaces the difference within minutes.
Should CI run tests against a real database?

For integration tests, yes, and GitLab makes it straightforward with service containers. Declare Postgres or Redis under services: and it runs alongside the job, reachable over the network with a clean state per job. That is considerably more trustworthy than mocking the database and finding out about a query problem in production. Keep unit tests free of external dependencies so they stay fast, and reserve service containers for the tests that genuinely need them.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Add security scanning to GitLab CI: SAST, DAST, secret detection, dependency and container scanning, and DevSecOps habits for secure pipelines.

GitLab CI security scanning is one of the fastest ways to bring DevSecOps into a real delivery workflow. Instead of treating security as a separate audit that happens after development is finished, DevSecOps makes security part of the pipeline itself. The same GitLab CI/CD process that builds, tests, and deploys your application can also run static analysis, scan dependencies, inspect container images, detect leaked secrets, and test a running application for common web vulnerabilities.

That approach is often described as shifting security left. The phrase means moving security checks earlier in the software lifecycle, closer to the moment code is written and reviewed. When a vulnerability is discovered during a merge request instead of in production, the cost of fixing it is dramatically lower. The developer still remembers the code change, the blast radius is smaller, and the team can fix the issue before it becomes part of a release.

GitLab is particularly strong here because it does not bolt security onto CI as an afterthought. It provides built-in security analyzers, security report formats, merge request widgets, dashboards, and vulnerability workflows. For teams building modern delivery pipelines, that makes GitLab a practical DevSecOps platform rather than just a CI runner.

sections.title: What DevSecOps Means in Practice
paragraphs: DevSecOps is not just “run a scanner sometimes.” It is a mindset and an operating model.

In a traditional workflow, development writes code, operations deploys it, and security reviews it near the end. That sequence creates friction. Security findings arrive late, release dates slip, and teams start seeing security as a blocker.

This is why “shift left” matters. The earlier a problem is identified, the cheaper it is to fix and the less likely it is to reach customers.

sections.title: GitLab Built-In Security Scanning Overview
paragraphs: GitLab provides a suite of security scanners and report integrations. Availability depends on your GitLab edition and tier. In general, GitLab Ultimate offers the richest security experience, especially for dashboards, governance, and vulnerability management, while some security capabilities and templates are available on Free or Premium as well.
The major scanners you will see in GitLab CI security scanning are:
The important idea is that each scanner looks at a different layer of risk:
No single scanner covers everything. The value comes from using multiple scanners together.

sections.title: SAST: Static Application Security Testing
paragraphs: Static Application Security Testing (SAST) analyzes source code without running the application. It looks for risky patterns, unsafe API usage, insecure coding constructs, and common weaknesses such as injection risks, weak cryptography usage, insecure deserialization, or insecure file handling.
Because SAST runs before deployment, it is one of the purest forms of shift-left security. It catches problems while developers are still working in branches and merge requests.

A GitLab SAST analyzer inspects the code repository and attempts to identify vulnerabilities in supported languages and frameworks. Depending on analyzer support and configuration, it can inspect languages such as:
The exact analyzer selection depends on the project contents. GitLab automatically chooses analyzers based on the repository language and the included SAST template.

sections.title: Secret Detection
paragraphs: One of the most common CI security failures is not a code vulnerability at all. It is a secret that accidentally got committed to Git: an API key, cloud credential, SSH private key, database password, access token, or webhook secret.

Once a secret lands in Git history, the problem is bigger than deleting it from the latest commit. The credential may already have been cloned, logged, mirrored, or exposed in a merge request. The correct response often includes revoking and rotating the secret.
GitLab Secret Detection looks for known secret patterns and high-risk tokens in the repository history or commit content, depending on configuration.

Secret detection is one of the highest-value scanners because it addresses a very common and very dangerous mistake. Even a mature team can accidentally commit a credential. Catching it in CI gives you a chance to stop the merge and rotate the secret before production risk grows.

sections.title: Dependency Scanning
paragraphs: Modern software depends heavily on open-source libraries. A Node.js application might use dozens or hundreds of transitive packages. A Python service may rely on libraries listed in requirements.txt or poetry.lock. A Java application may pull dependencies through Maven or Gradle. Those libraries save time, but they also introduce supply-chain risk.
Dependency Scanning checks manifest and lock files against vulnerability databases to identify packages with known CVEs or advisories.

Dependency scanning is also valuable after a merge. New CVEs are published every day. A package that looked fine last month may become high risk today. Running dependency scans regularly helps you spot those changes.

That improves adoption because developers do not have to leave the review flow and open a separate security tool. The feedback is attached to the change they are reviewing.

sections.title: Failing the Pipeline on Severity Thresholds
paragraphs: Running scans is good. Enforcing policy is better.
Many teams eventually want a rule such as:

There are several ways to enforce that, depending on your GitLab tier and governance model. At a basic level, you can make security jobs required and use merge request approval or policy features. Another practical approach is to add a custom gate job that reads generated report artifacts and exits non-zero when the threshold is exceeded.
A simplified example for SAST might look like this:

      echo "High or critical SAST findings: $critical_or_high"
      test "$critical_or_high" -eq 0

sections.title: Final Takeaway
paragraphs: GitLab CI security scanning turns security from a late manual review into an automated part of delivery. SAST checks source code, Secret Detection catches leaked credentials, Dependency Scanning finds vulnerable packages, Container Scanning inspects image layers, and DAST probes a running application. Together, they create a practical DevSecOps workflow that helps teams shift security left without leaving the GitLab pipeline experience.

If you are just getting started, enable SAST and Secret Detection first. Once the team gets comfortable with GitLab security reports, add dependency, container, and dynamic scanning. That step-by-step path is how many strong DevSecOps programs begin.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What security scanners does GitLab include?

SAST analyses your source code for vulnerable patterns, Secret Detection looks for credentials committed to the repository, Dependency Scanning checks your declared dependencies against known CVEs, Container Scanning inspects built images for vulnerable operating system packages, and DAST exercises a running application for runtime issues. They are enabled by including GitLab's templates in your pipeline. Availability of the merge request widget, the security dashboard and vulnerability management varies by GitLab tier, though the scanners themselves run on all of them.
Which scanner should I enable first?

Secret Detection, because a leaked credential is an immediate and unambiguous problem, and because it finds things regardless of language or framework. Dependency Scanning is a close second, since most vulnerabilities in a typical application arrive through its dependencies rather than its own code. SAST is valuable but noisier, and is best introduced once the team has capacity to triage findings. Adding all five at once usually produces a volume of results nobody acts on.
Should I fail the pipeline on security findings?

On critical and high severity findings in new code, yes. On everything, no. A policy of zero findings gets disabled within a month because it blocks unrelated work on pre-existing issues. A practical approach is to fail only on new critical and high vulnerabilities introduced by the change, report the rest without blocking, and work through the existing backlog separately. GitLab's merge request widget shows newly introduced findings specifically, which is what makes this distinction workable.
What is the difference between SAST and DAST?

SAST reads your source code without running it, so it can point at an exact file and line and runs early and fast in the pipeline. DAST attacks a running instance of the application from the outside, so it finds issues that only appear at runtime. Configuration problems, authentication flaws, injection that depends on real request handling, but it needs a deployed environment and takes much longer. They find genuinely different classes of problem and complement each other rather than competing.
Secret Detection found a credential in an old commit. Is removing it from the code enough?

No. Git history is permanent, so anyone with repository access can still read the secret from the earlier commit, and any clone already contains it. Treat it as compromised: rotate the credential immediately, then remove it from the current code. Rewriting history to purge it is possible but disruptive and does not help if the repository was ever public or cloned. Rotation is the step that actually restores security; history cleanup is housekeeping.
How do I stop security scanning slowing every pipeline down?

Run the heavier scanners where they earn their keep rather than on every commit. Secret Detection and Dependency Scanning are fast enough to run everywhere. Container Scanning naturally belongs after the image is built, and DAST needs a deployed environment so it fits on merge requests to the default branch or on a nightly schedule. Using rules to target them appropriately keeps the fast feedback loop fast while still getting the coverage.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Deploy to AWS from GitLab CI using OIDC instead of static keys, then ship to S3 and EC2, push images to ECR, update ECS services and automate Terraform runs.

Deploying to AWS from GitLab CI/CD is one of the most common real-world automation patterns in modern DevOps. GitLab builds and tests your application, and AWS provides the infrastructure or managed platform where the application runs. When combined well, you get repeatable, auditable, environment-aware deployments that do not rely on someone manually running commands from a laptop.

A GitLab CI deploy to AWS pipeline can be simple or advanced. At the simple end, a pipeline might upload a static website to Amazon S3. At the advanced end, the pipeline might build a container image, push it to Amazon ECR, update an ECS task definition, roll a new service deployment, and manage supporting infrastructure with Terraform.
The foundation of all of these patterns is the same: GitLab CI needs a secure way to authenticate to AWS. Once authentication is solved, the rest becomes a matter of pipeline design.

sections.title: Overview of Deploying to AWS from GitLab CI
paragraphs: There is no single “AWS deployment” workflow. AWS offers many targets, and GitLab can drive all of them. Common patterns include:
Your choice depends on the application architecture.

sections.title: AWS Credential Management: Access Keys vs OIDC
paragraphs: The most important design decision is how GitLab CI will obtain AWS credentials.
The older pattern is to create an IAM user, generate an AWS access key ID and AWS secret access key, and store them as GitLab CI/CD variables. This works, but it has drawbacks:
Long-lived keys are acceptable for small labs or legacy pipelines, but they are no longer the best default.

A better modern pattern is OIDC (OpenID Connect). With OIDC, GitLab issues an identity token to the job, AWS trusts that token through an IAM OIDC provider, and the job assumes an IAM role using temporary credentials.
That is better because:
In short, if you are designing a new GitLab CI deploy to AWS workflow, OIDC is usually the better choice.

sections.title: Using AWS Access Keys in GitLab CI/CD Variables
paragraphs: If you must use access keys, store them in GitLab CI/CD variables rather than hardcoding them in .gitlab-ci.yml.
The common variables are:
A simple job might look like this:
The AWS CLI automatically reads AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, and AWS_DEFAULT_REGION from the environment.
This approach is straightforward, but remember the trade-off: the key is still a secret you must protect and rotate.
